SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology01 / 19
Quick Review

Sociology studies human lives by examining their locations in the social contexts, using sociological imagination and scientific tools.

The Sociology Imagination involves viewing individual experiences through the social contexts that shape those experiences.

The Sociological Imagination enables us to grasp the connection between history and biography

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology04 / 19
Take a Perspective

In sociology, a theoretical perspective or theoretical paradigm, is defined as an overall view or image of society.

It offers a lens through which we see the society; (from some perspectives we see things that we fail to see from other perspectives)

Different perspectives yield different images of the society

Think about the sun glass!

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology05 / 19
Theory & Theoretical Perspective

Theory: “scientific theory”, “middle-range theory”;

E.g., the germ theory; the cumulative inequality theory, …

Theoretical Perspective: “grand theory”, “paradigm”;

E.g., Evolution Theory; Creation Theory

A (scientific) theory is a posteriori, empirical, and can be falsified; A theoretical perspective is a priori, interpretive, and cannot be falsified.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology07 / 19
1. Structural Functionalism

The central Idea: 1. Society is a whole unit (like a human body), made up of interrelated parts/organs (the structure);

2. Each part of society contributes to the survival of the whole (function).

Auguste Comte Herbert Spencer Emile Durkheim

(1798-1857) (1820-1903) (1858-1917)

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology08 / 19
1. Structural Functionalism

An Organic (or Wholistic) View of Society! (society like a body)

The “structure”: how the parts of a society fit together to make the whole

The “function”: what each part does, how it contributes to society

E.g.: Factories in the 19th century, with all the human miseries happening in them, are necessary parts functioning for the benefit of the evolution of society.

E.g.: Modern day sweatshops in developing countries are necessary parts functioning for the world economic system.

The classical version of this perspective has limitations in explaining social changes!

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology09 / 19
Development of Structural Functionalism

Robert K. Merton (1910-2003):

Function vs. Dysfunction;

Manifest Function/Dysfunction vs. Latent Function/Dysfunction

Manifest function/dysfunction: obvious, intended consequences;

Latent function/dysfunction: consequences unintended but still happen

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology10 / 19
1. Structural Functionalism

Emphasizes social integration and social order

A communitarian orientation and a conservative inclination

“The individual submits to society and this submission is the condition of his liberation. For man freedom consists in deliverance from blind, unthinking physical forces; he achieves this by opposing against them the great and intelligent force of society, under whose protection he shelters. By putting himself under the wing of society, he makes himself also, to a certain extent, dependent upon it. But this is a liberating dependence; there is no contradiction in this”.

“The outcome of rebellion against the norms … is a perpetual agony of indecision linked to a state of uncertainty about the intentions and moves of others around - likely to make life a living hell”.

Changes should be gradual and organic.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology11 / 19
2. Conflict Theory

Conflict theory pictures society as being fragmented into groups that are competing with one another for scarce resources.

Social order is maintained not by consensus but by domination and coercion, with power in the hands of those with the greatest political, economic, and social resources.

The founder?

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology12 / 19
2. Conflict Theory

Conflict theory pictures society as being fragmented into groups that are competing with one another for scarce resources.

Social order is maintained not by consensus but by domination and coercion, with power in the hands of those with the greatest political, economic, and social resources.

The founder: Karl Marx (1818–1883)

Das Kapital

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology13 / 19
2. Conflict Theory:

A conflict history of humanity

Slavery: Slave-owner vs. Slave

Feudalism: Aristocracy vs. Peasants

Capitalism: Bourgeoisie vs. Proletariat

A categorically paired view of society!

A Conflictual View of Society!

The Classical Version

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology14 / 19
2. Conflict Theory: The Classical Version

The self-destruction of Capitalism:

Landlords turned into Capitalists (Bourgeoisie): The take land from peasants to convert it to plants or factory farms; they invest their wealth in industries.

Peasants join the industry labor force and become part of the proletariat;

The Bourgeoisie are eager to improve the way work is organized and to adopt innovations allow them to produce more efficiently, earn high profits, and need less human labors;

The reduced need for human labors leads to lower wages; Profits also drives capitalists to concentrate workers in larger and larger facilities, keep wages as low as possible;

Labors lost their humanity but were reduced to an extension of machines;

The Proletariat is growing bigger and bigger, their living conditions became more and more miserable, and finally it will overthrown the exploiters ----the capitalists.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology15 / 19
2. Conflict Theory: The Classical Version

How the powerful retain their power?

Through Forces; (“The executive of the modern state is nothing but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie.” -------- The Communist Manifesto)

Through a belief system legitimizing the current system (a “false consciousness” for the dominated): something would be taken for granted by the dominated but in fact are serving the interest of the dominating.

The working class struggle today

Original visual slide

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology17 / 19
2. Conflict Theory: The Modern Version

Extended beyond the relationship of capitalists and workers.

Examples: whites vs. blacks; men vs. women; giant cooperates vs. individual investors; industrialized nations vs. non-industrialized nations; religion vs. religion; civilization vs. civilization; teachers vs. students; parents vs. teenagers; senior employees vs. junior employees, ….

In a nutshell, it could happen between any categorical pairs with competing interests and yet asymmetrical positions.

It always involves struggling for POWER!

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology18 / 19
2. Conflict Theory

Emphasizes social inequality and power struggle

A revolutionary orientation and a radical inclination

“Let the ruling classes tremble at a Communist revolution. The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win”.

“Struggles of masses and ideas. An epic that will be carried forward by our peoples, mistreated and scorned by imperialism; our people, unreckoned with until today, who are now beginning to shake off their slumber. Imperialism considered us a weak and submissive flock; and now it begins to be terrified of that flock...”.

“Political power grows out of the barrel of a gun”.

Changes are achieved through power struggle, which can be dramatic and violent.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology19 / 19
3. Symbolic Interactionism

Symbolic interactionism views a society as being composed of interactions among its members, which are based on symbols with meanings.

Three tenets:

Human beings act towards things based on the meanings those things have for them;

Such meanings arise out of the interaction of the individual with others;

Interpretation of meanings is influenced by specific context.

An interactive view of society!
